what_it_does: Modern mobile phones run complex apps (interpreters, UI frameworks, JavaScript runtimes) with so much code that the CPU's instruction cache keeps evicting the most-used pieces — causing the processor to stall waiting for code to reload even after standard compiler optimizations are applied. TRRIP solves this by letting the compiler label code as 'hot', 'warm', or 'cold' based on profiling data, passing those labels all the way down to the cache hardware, which then keeps hot code pinned in cache longer and pushes cold code out faster. The result is 26.5% fewer cache misses for instructions and a 3.9% average speedup — essentially for free, with no extra chip area required.
method_in_detail:
The idea. A CPU's instruction cache (a small, fast on-chip storage holding recently used program code) can only keep a limited amount of code at once. When code is too varied, the cache fills up and important frequently-run code gets evicted. The hardware alone can't tell which code matters most; it only sees recent accesses. The compiler, however, already knows from profiling (running the app and counting which code runs most often) which functions are 'hot' (executed constantly), 'warm', or 'cold' (rarely touched).

How it works. TRRIP is a three-layer team effort: compiler, operating system, and cache hardware.

1. Compiler step: LLVM (a widely-used open-source compiler) runs the app with typical inputs, counts how often each small code block executes, and labels everything hot, warm, or cold. It then places all hot code in a special section of the program binary (.text.hot), warm code in another (.text.warm), and cold code in a third. Just physically separating cold from hot code already improves performance by keeping them from bumping into each other in the cache.

2. Operating system step: When the OS loads the program into memory, it reads those section labels and writes a 2-bit 'temperature' tag into each memory page's page-table entry (a small bookkeeping record the OS maintains for every chunk of memory). ARM processors already reserve spare bits in these records (called PBHA bits) for exactly this kind of custom metadata — so no hardware changes are needed to store the tag.

3. Cache hardware step: Each time the CPU fetches an instruction, its memory translation unit reads those temperature bits from the page table and attaches them to the memory request. The cache replacement policy (TRRIP, an extension of an existing algorithm called RRIP — Re-Reference Interval Prediction) reads this temperature label on every incoming cache line. Hot lines are inserted at the highest priority (they are treated as if they were just recently used, so they survive eviction longest). Warm lines get second-highest priority. Cold lines and data follow the original RRIP default, which inserts them at lower priority.

The key design choice. Instead of adding any new chip storage or new CPU instructions, TRRIP reuses spare bits that already exist in ARM processors. This makes adoption essentially free in terms of hardware cost.

The result. Across 10 mobile-proxy benchmarks already optimized by standard profiling, TRRIP reduces L2 instruction-cache misses by 26.5% and delivers a geometric-mean 3.9% speedup — beating all evaluated hardware-only alternatives (CLIP, Emissary, SHiP) while adding ~0% area and power overhead.
